abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel paradigm for motion synthesis in virtual characters by integrating Riemannian manifold theory with deep reinforcement learning, fundamentally redefining how motion data is represented and generated in computer animation. Traditional approaches treat motion capture data as isolated poses in Euclidean space, failing to capture the intrinsic geometric structure of human movement. Our method models the space of natural human motions as a curved manifold embedded in high-dimensional pose space, where geodesic distances accurately measure motion similarity and transition costs. We propose a manifold-aware policy architecture that learns to navigate this geometric structure, enabling characters to generate stylistically coherent and physically plausible motions without explicit motion blending or interpolation. Experimental evaluation on complex character animation tasks demonstrates that our paradigm produces qualitatively superior results compared to state-of-the-art methods, particularly in scenarios requiring long-horizon motion planning and stylistic consistency. The theoretical framework we introduce provides a unified mathematical language for understanding motion synthesis problems, opening new research directions in expressive animation and virtual storytelling. This work bridges the gap between differential geometry and character animation, establishing manifold-based reasoning as a foundational paradigm for next-generation computer animation systems.

This paper presents a theoretically grounded improvement to physics-based character animation through a novel symplectic integration framework with adaptive energy conservation. Existing physics engines employ semi-implicit Euler or naive Verlet methods that introduce systematic energy drift during long simulation sequences, degrading animation quality in interactive virtual environments. We develop a novel formulation based on constrained Hamiltonian mechanics that preserves system energy exactly while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for real-time applications. Our approach introduces energy-momentum conserving constraints that handle contact and friction without artificial damping, preserving the physical authenticity of character motion in virtual worlds. The theoretical analysis establishes rigorous bounds on energy error propagation and demonstrates superior stability compared to existing methods. Quantitative evaluation on standard physics-based animation benchmarks shows significant improvements in motion fidelity and energy conservation, with up to 73% reduction in energy drift. This work provides a principled theoretical foundation for developing robust physics-based animation systems, enabling more believable character interactions in real-time animation applications ranging from game animation to virtual reality experiences.

We present CrowdFlow, a groundbreaking crowd simulation system that achieves real-time emergent behavior through a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning architecture. Unlike traditional crowd simulation approaches relying on simplified behavioral rules or optimization-based path planning, our system enables realistic emergent group dynamics including lane formation, pedestrian flows, and collective panic behaviors in virtual environments. The architecture employs a novel attention-based communication protocol that allows agents to coordinate without centralized control, scaling to thousands of simultaneous virtual characters while maintaining real-time performance. Our system integrates seamlessly with modern game engines and virtual reality platforms, providing interactive simulation capabilities for applications ranging from urban planning visualization to immersive training scenarios. Extensive evaluation demonstrates that CrowdFlow produces qualitatively distinct and behaviorally valid crowd phenomena that cannot emerge from rule-based systems, fundamentally changing how interactive virtual worlds handle population-scale simulations. The system architecture prioritizes extensibility, allowing researchers to incorporate domain-specific behavioral models while benefiting from the core emergent coordination capabilities. This work establishes a new paradigm for crowd simulation in computer animation, moving beyond scripted behaviors toward truly autonomous virtual populations.

This paper presents MotionSync, an improved interactive animation system for real-time character control in augmented reality applications. Existing interactive animation systems suffer from significant latency, poor pose estimation accuracy, and lack of semantic understanding when mapping user movements to virtual avatars. Our system introduces a lightweight neural pose estimator that achieves sub-10ms latency while maintaining high-fidelity tracking suitable for expressive animation requirements. The architecture employs a hierarchical temporal attention mechanism that predicts intended character poses from incomplete and noisy input, enabling robust performance under varying capture conditions common in mobile augmented reality scenarios. We designed an adaptive blending module that smoothly transitions between procedural animation and user-driven poses, producing natural character motion that respects physical constraints in virtual worlds. Implementation details include optimization strategies for mobile GPU architectures, enabling sustained 60fps performance on consumer devices. User studies with 48 participants demonstrate significant improvements in perceived animation quality, system responsiveness, and presence compared to baseline methods. MotionSync provides a practical solution for developers seeking to create compelling avatar-based experiences in augmented reality, advancing the state-of-the-art for interactive animation in portable devices.
